opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are a few layers of challenges, and they're quite different in nature.

The first is data scarcity. Compared to natural language math, or even to code in Python, the amount of formalized mathematics in Lean is tiny. Mathlib is a remarkable community achievement, but it's on the order of a few hundred thousand theorems, and it's heavily concentrated in certain areas, like algebra, topology, and parts of analysis, while other areas are barely touched. So if you want a model that can prove things in Lean, you can't just do the usual thing of scraping the internet and pretraining. You have to think about how to generate data: autoformalization, translating informal textbook and paper proofs into Lean, and self-play, where the system proposes conjectures, tries to prove them, and learns from both successes and failures. Each of those has its own pitfalls. Autoformalization can produce statements that type-check but don't actually mean what the original theorem meant. That's a subtle and dangerous failure mode, because the verifier says "correct," but it's correct about the wrong thing.

The second challenge is the gap between how mathematicians think and how Lean wants you to write. A human proof might say "by a standard compactness argument" or "without loss of generality," and that's one line. In Lean, it could be fifty lines, and you need to know exactly which lemma in Mathlib has the right name and the right hypotheses in the right form. A lot of the difficulty is less deep mathematics and more library navigation: premise selection, retrieving the right lemma out of hundreds of thousands, dealing with coercions, typeclass issues, and definitional unfolding. Models are often good at the high-level idea and then get stuck on these low-level frictions.

Third is search and credit assignment. Proving is a long-horizon problem. You might make a hundred tactic steps, and the only reward signal is at the very end: the proof compiles or it doesn't. So you need good search, good value estimates for intermediate proof states, and the ability to decompose a hard theorem into lemmas, prove the lemmas, and reassemble. Getting the system to plan at the level of lemmas, the way a mathematician sketches a proof strategy before filling details, is, I think, one of the most important open problems.

Fourth, there's the infrastructure side, which people underestimate. Lean compilation is not free. When you're doing reinforcement learning at scale, you're running enormous numbers of proof attempts, and each needs to be checked. Mathlib also evolves constantly; lemmas get renamed and refactored, so a model trained on one version can break on another. Building a fast, stable, parallel verification environment is real engineering work.

And finally, there's the question of what we actually want. Competition problems like IMO are a good benchmark, but research mathematics is different. It involves new definitions and building theory, not just proving a given statement. A system that can introduce the right abstractions, formalize them, and make them useful is a much harder target than one that solves a fixed problem.

But the reason I'm excited about Lean despite all this is that verification gives you something very rare in AI: a perfectly reliable reward signal. You don't need a human grader, and you can't hallucinate your way to a passing proof. That makes mathematics in Lean, I think, one of the best testbeds for building AI that genuinely reasons rather than just sounds like it does.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the first thing to say is that Lean changes the nature of the problem. When you're doing informal mathematics, "proving" something means convincing a human reader, and there's a lot of hand-waving that mathematicians accept as standard. In Lean, the checker accepts nothing. Every step has to be justified down to the axioms, through the library. So the challenge isn't really "can the model reason," it's "can the model reason and produce something that a very unforgiving compiler will accept."

The biggest technical challenge, honestly, is the library. Mathlib is enormous and growing, and the gap between what a mathematician would say in one sentence and what exists as a lemma in Mathlib can be huge. Sometimes a trivial-sounding fact just isn't there, or it's there under a name and in a form you'd never guess. So a system has to be very good at retrieval, at knowing what tools already exist, and it also has to be able to build its own intermediate lemmas when the library doesn't have what it needs. That second part is where a lot of systems fail. They can pattern-match to existing lemmas but they can't construct the scaffolding for a genuinely new argument.

The second challenge is the search space. A proof in Lean is a tree of tactic applications, and at each node you have an enormous number of possible moves, most of them useless. Naive search explodes. So the real work is in guidance: how do you get a model to propose a small number of promising steps, and how do you allocate compute across branches? There's a tension there between depth and breadth. Competition-style problems might need a long chain of fairly standard steps, while research-style problems might need one creative idea and then a lot of routine verification. A system that's tuned for one tends to be bad at the other.

Third is the feedback loop. One advantage of Lean is that you get an exact error signal — the compiler tells you where it broke. But those error messages are not always informative in the way a model needs. A type mismatch deep in a coercion can look like noise. Teaching a model to actually learn from that feedback, rather than just retrying randomly, is something we spend a lot of time on.

And then there's a data problem underneath all of this. There isn't that much formal proof data compared to natural language or code. So a lot of the progress comes from autoformalization — taking informal mathematics and translating it into Lean — and from self-play-style loops where the system generates problems, attempts them, and keeps the verified proofs as training data. The nice thing about Lean is that verification is free and trustworthy, so you never train on something false. But generating problems that are both hard enough to be useful and actually well-formed is its own challenge. A lot of auto-generated formal statements are either trivially true, trivially false, or just not what the informal statement meant.

Finally I'd say there's an engineering challenge that people underestimate: Lean itself is slow to check at scale, Mathlib changes constantly, and keeping a reinforcement learning loop stable on top of a moving target is genuinely hard. A surprising fraction of the work is infrastructure, not modeling.

But I'm optimistic. The thing that makes Lean exciting is exactly that it's strict. If the system says it has a proof, you can trust that it does. That's a very different kind of guarantee than anything else in AI right now.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the biggest challenges is bridging the gap between how mathematicians write proofs and what Lean needs to check them. On paper, we routinely skip steps that seem obvious. In Lean, those steps have to be justified, either explicitly or through automation. So a system needs to understand not just the broad mathematical idea, but all the details that make it valid.

Then there’s the search problem. At any point in a proof, you might introduce a definition, apply a lemma, or prove an intermediate statement. Which move actually helps? Finding the right result in a large library—and recognizing that it applies even when it’s expressed differently—is a substantial challenge.

Lean gives you a very useful feedback loop: you can propose a step and check it. But knowing that a step failed doesn’t necessarily tell you what the right strategy is. The harder task is turning that feedback into progress, especially for proofs that require a new construction or a sequence of intermediate lemmas.

So I’d distinguish between generating something that looks like a mathematical proof and building a system that can reliably develop a proof that Lean accepts. Closing that gap requires mathematical reasoning, effective search, and good engineering around the verifier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the biggest challenges is the gap between how mathematicians communicate proofs and what Lean actually needs. A mathematician might say, “This follows immediately,” but that sentence can hide a lot of work: choosing the right representation, finding the relevant lemma, and checking that all the assumptions line up. A proving system has to make those steps explicit.

There’s also a search problem. Even if the mathematical idea is right, there are many possible intermediate steps, and most won’t help. The system needs to recognize when to use an existing theorem, when to introduce a new lemma, and when to change its approach. Finding the right result in a large library is itself a significant challenge.

Lean gives you a very useful feedback loop because it can check whether a proof is correct. But turning an error message into a productive next step is much harder than simply knowing that an attempt failed. And as proofs get longer, you need to manage dependencies and maintain a coherent strategy across many steps.

So I’d distinguish producing a proof that Lean accepts from finding the mathematical ideas that make that proof possible. The checker gives us a precise standard of correctness; building a system that can reliably discover those ideas is the harder part.
